howToRefresh: Ingest the KY History morning email to public/content/raw-briefs/YYYY-MM-DD.md, run npm run parse-briefs, then npm run build (includes build-home-preview). The homepage also re-reads stories.json in the browser.

stories.title: Sassafras Ridge (15Fu3): Mississippian town on the western border
stories.summary: Sassafras Ridge (15Fu3) in Fulton County was one of the Mississippian mound towns of far western Kentucky, occupied in roughly AD 1000–1500.
stories.quote: Sassafras Ridge (site 15Fu3) is a Mississippian mound center in Fulton County, in the far western corner of Kentucky near the Mississippi River.

photo.title: Mound A at Wickliffe Mounds, Ballard County (photographed 2008); stand-in, since Sassafras Ridge is address-restricted and no public photo is used
photo.attribution: Chris Light · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

stories.heroDeck: Sassafras Ridge (site 15Fu3) is a Mississippian mound center in Fulton County, in the far western corner of Kentucky near the Mississippi River.

stories.title: Col. Thomas Marshall at Buck Pond
stories.summary: Col. Thomas Marshall (1730–1802), Revolutionary officer and father of Chief Justice John Marshall, ran Virginia’s military-land survey office in Kentucky and founded Buck Pond near Versailles.
stories.quote: Col. Thomas Marshall (1730–1802) came to Kentucky as a veteran of two wars and a surveyor by trade.

photo.title: Col. Thomas Marshall, the only known portrait, as reproduced in Albert J. Beveridge’s Life of John Marshall
photo.attribution: Unknown artist · reproduced by Albert J. Beveridge · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: Col. Thomas Marshall (1730–1802) came to Kentucky as a veteran of two wars and a surveyor by trade.

stories.title: Moluntha and Logan’s Raid, 1786
stories.summary: In October 1786 Kentucky militia under Benjamin Logan burned Shawnee towns in Ohio, and Hugh McGary killed the aged Mekoche Shawnee leader Moluntha after he surrendered under an American flag.
stories.quote: Moluntha (died 1786), also spelled Melonthe or Malunthy, was a civil chief of the Mekoche division of the Shawnee.

photo.title: Map of Logan’s Raid into the Ohio Country, 1786 (modern map, 2021); no portrait of Moluntha is known
photo.attribution: Kevin1776 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

stories.heroDeck: Moluntha (died 1786), also spelled Melonthe or Malunthy, was a civil chief of the Mekoche division of the Shawnee.

stories.title: Prestonsburg: first seat on the Big Sandy
stories.summary: Laid out as Preston’s Station in 1797 on the Levisa Fork, Prestonsburg became the seat of a vast new Floyd County in 1800 and was formally established in 1818.
stories.quote: Prestonsburg sits on the Levisa Fork of the Big Sandy, on land that was part of a 100,000-acre colonial grant to the family of Elizabeth Patton Preston.

photo.title: Samuel May House, Prestonsburg (built 1817; photographed 2014)
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: Prestonsburg sits on the Levisa Fork of the Big Sandy, on land that was part of a 100,000-acre colonial grant to the family of Elizabeth Patton Preston.

stories.title: George Garvin Brown and Old Forester
stories.summary: In 1870 Louisville’s George Garvin Brown began selling Old Forester only in sealed glass bottles, a guarantee against watered whiskey that became the foundation of Brown-Forman.
stories.quote: George Garvin Brown was born in Munfordville on September 2, 1846, and moved to Louisville in 1862.

photo.title: J. T. S. Brown and Son’s Complex on East Main Street, Louisville (photographed 2012), part of the Brown family’s whiskey district; stand-in, not the Old Forester building at 119 W. Main
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: George Garvin Brown was born in Munfordville on September 2, 1846, and moved to Louisville in 1862.

layers.name: Big Bone Lick
layers.blurb: A Pleistocene salt lick where mastodons left bones in the mud — Kentucky’s window on deep time.

photo.attribution: Mattguyver · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

layers.blurb: Flagship Kentucky Historical Society museum, covering more than 12,000 years of the Commonwealth.

photo.attribution: Jon698 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0

layers.name: Blue Licks Battlefield
layers.wiki: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park
layers.blurb: August 19, 1782: the last major Revolutionary War battle in Kentucky.

photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Old Talbott Tavern
layers.blurb: Court Square tavern since the late 1700s — among America’s oldest inns, still a working bourbon bar.

layers.name: Goddard Covered Bridge
layers.blurb: White Bridge: a Town-lattice span over Sand Lick Creek, among Kentucky’s surviving covered bridges.

photo.attribution: Greg Hume · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Bourbon Iron Works
layers.blurb: Jacob Myers blew in a charcoal blast furnace here in 1791 — munitions for the early Commonwealth.

photo.title: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
photo.attribution: Jeff Bates · HABS / Library of Congress · Public domain

layers.name: The Kentucke Gazette
layers.blurb: Kentucky’s first newspaper, begun August 11, 1787 by John and Fielding Bradford.

photo.title: Kentucke Gazette printing house
photo.attribution: William Henry Perrin / Filson Club · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Cumberland Falls
layers.blurb: The “Niagara of the South,” and one of the few Western Hemisphere places a moonbow can appear.

photo.attribution: Aaron Vowels · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0

layers.name: Frankfort Cemetery
layers.blurb: Hilltop rural cemetery (1844) overlooking the capital — Daniel and Rebecca Boone were reinterred here.

layers.blurb: A Kentucky River distilling campus with late-1700s roots, continuous through Prohibition.
